prompt: Which steps did fake-gestures.mjs send for the swipe made by hand?
hint: Look at the five lines under "swipe by hand".

choices.text: A single swipe command carrying a direction and a distance
choices.why: The protocol has no swipe command; a swipe is described as what a finger does.

choices.text: pointerMove, pointerDown, pause, pointerMove, pointerUp
choices.why: Right. To the start, touch, wait, move over 400 ms, lift.

choices.text: A pointerDown at the start and a pointerUp at the end
choices.why: Without a pointerMove in between, the finger would lift where it touched: that is a tap.

choices.text: Two clicks, one at each end
choices.why: A click is a separate request on an element; nothing was clicked in the swipe.

prompt: A test swipes up on Tickets's list. Which way do the rows go?
hint: Whose direction does "up" name?

choices.text: Down, back towards the first row
choices.why: That is the list's direction taken for the finger's, the commonest gesture bug.

choices.text: Up, with the finger
choices.why: Right. The direction is the finger's, and the content follows it.

choices.text: Nowhere: a list needs a scroll command
choices.why: A scroll is a swipe on a scrollable view; the list moves.

choices.text: Sideways, since the list is vertical
choices.why: A vertical swipe moves a vertical list along its own axis.

prompt: In the run, driver.swipe() with percent 0.5 put the finger down at which y coordinate?
hint: The first pointerMove under "driver.swipe()".

prompt: Match each gesture to the pointer steps that make it.
hint: The paragraph under the table of steps.

pairs.right: down and up at one point
down, a pause of about a second, up
down, a move with a duration, up

prompt: Why would a suite that runs on Android and iOS keep to W3C actions rather than mobile swipeGesture?
hint: Look at what the fake driver answered.

choices.text: W3C actions are faster on Android
choices.why: Speed is not the difference; the mobile gestures are often the steadier ones on Android.

choices.text: mobile swipeGesture needs pixel coordinates
choices.why: It takes an element and a percentage; the actions are the ones that need coordinates.

choices.text: A mobile command belongs to one driver
choices.why: Right. The fake driver refused it as unsupported; the XCUITest driver has its own set.

choices.text: WebdriverIO does not send execute requests
choices.why: It sent one in the run, and the fake driver answered it with the error.

prompt: Who draws the dialog that asks whether Tickets may send notifications?
hint: It is drawn on top of the app's window.

choices.text: ShowActivity, from its layout
choices.why: The layout has the switch and the line; the app only asks, with requestPermissions.

choices.text: Android's permission controller
choices.why: Right. A system app draws it, which is why its ids carry another package.

choices.text: The UiAutomator2 driver, to let a test answer it
choices.why: The driver can see it; it does not create it.

choices.text: Appium's server, when the session asks
choices.why: The server only forwards commands; the dialog appears on a phone with no test at all.

prompt: Why can an Espresso test not press Don't allow on the notification dialog?
hint: Where does an Espresso test act?

choices.text: Espresso has no action for buttons
choices.why: click() presses any view it finds; the problem is finding this one.

choices.text: The dialog's buttons have no ids
choices.why: They have ids, in the permission controller's package, which Appium uses.

choices.text: The dialog closes before Espresso looks
choices.why: It stays until somebody answers it; that is what the Appium test waits for.

choices.text: It is a window of another app
choices.why: Right. Espresso acts on the windows of the app it runs in.

prompt: reminder.test.mjs is run against an emulator with Android 12. What happens?
hint: Line 32 of ShowActivity.kt.

choices.text: Both pass, since the switch turns on
choices.why: The switch does turn on, but each test first waits for a dialog that never comes.

choices.text: Both fail, waiting for the dialog
choices.why: Right. Below API 33 the app asks nothing, so waitUntilShown times out in both.

choices.text: The Allow test passes and the other fails
choices.why: Both start with the same wait for the dialog, so both stop there.

choices.text: Android 12 shows the same dialog
choices.why: Notifications became a runtime permission in Android 13.

prompt: Which of these leave Tickets in a state where the next tap on the switch shows the dialog?
hint: The dialog appears only when the permission has never been answered.

choices.text: Uninstalling and installing the app again
choices.why: Right. A fresh install has no memory of earlier answers.

choices.text: mobile removeApp followed by mobile installApp
choices.why: Right. It is the same fresh install, from Appium, as the test's beforeEach does.

choices.text: adb shell pm grant for POST_NOTIFICATIONS
choices.why: The permission is then granted, and line 33 returns without asking.

choices.text: The capability appium:autoGrantPermissions set to true
choices.why: It installs with every permission granted, which removes the dialog.

choices.text: Refusing it twice before
choices.why: After two refusals Android stops showing the dialog and refuses at once.

prompt: Notifications need the person's permission, asked at runtime, from Android ___ on.
hint: SDK_INT 33.

prompt: The phone is turned while ShowActivity is on screen. What does Android do with the activity?
hint: A rotation is a configuration change.

choices.text: It keeps it and redraws the views
choices.why: That would keep remind_denied; the activity is destroyed instead.

choices.text: Destroys it and makes another
choices.why: Right. The new one gets the intent and the state the views saved.

choices.text: Kills the process and starts the app again
choices.why: The process stays; that is why Shows.baseUrl survives a rotation.

choices.text: Goes back to the list screen
choices.why: The show's screen is rebuilt where it was.

pairs.left: the saved copy of the list
pairs.right: kept through everything but an uninstall

pairs.left: the reminder switch, after a rotation

prompt: What separates adb shell am force-stop from adb shell am kill for a test of app states?
hint: Which one is a decision of the person?

choices.text: Nothing: both end the process
choices.why: Both end it; only one lets Android restore the screens afterwards.

choices.text: kill also removes the app's data
choices.why: Neither touches the data; clearing it is pm clear.

choices.text: Only kill lets Android rebuild the screens
choices.why: Right. force-stop is Force stop in the settings, a person ending the app; kill is what Android does for memory.

choices.text: force-stop works only while the app is in front
choices.why: It works in any state; kill is the one limited to the background.

prompt: Why did Appium 3 refuse to start with --allow-insecure adb_shell?
hint: Read the error line.

choices.text: Appium 3 no longer has a shell feature
choices.why: It has; the second start enabled it as uiautomator2:adb_shell.

choices.text: The feature must be named together with its driver
choices.why: Right. Appium 3 wants uiautomator2:adb_shell, or the wildcard, before the colon.

choices.text: A shell needs the server on every interface
choices.why: The accepted start listened on 127.0.0.1, which is the safer choice.

choices.text: No device was attached to run a shell on
choices.why: The check ran before any device was looked for; the error is about the name.

prompt: What part of a process death does ActivityScenario's recreate() not reproduce?
hint: Which process does the new activity live in?

choices.text: The state the views saved for themselves
choices.why: recreate() hands it to the new activity, as a process death does.

choices.text: Objects such as Shows starting again from scratch
choices.why: Right. The process stays, so Shows keeps its baseUrl and its busy counter.

choices.text: onCreate running a second time
choices.why: It runs again; that is the second load the idling resource waits for.

choices.text: The extras that came in the intent
choices.why: The new activity gets the same intent in both cases.

prompt: Why is the rotation test of states.test.mjs marked todo instead of left as a plain test?
hint: What does todo change in the report?

choices.text: So that node skips it until the defect is fixed
choices.why: A todo test still runs and its result is printed; it just does not fail the suite.

choices.text: Because it does not run on an emulator
choices.why: It runs on the emulator of lesson 14; it is expected to fail there.

choices.text: It checks a known, unfixed defect
choices.why: Right. It runs and reports, without turning the suite red for a reason everybody knows.

choices.text: Because it needs the insecure shell feature
choices.why: That is the other test, the process death, and it is not marked.

prompt: In the process-death test, which number must mobile queryAppState answer after am kill?
hint: The table of section 04.

prompt: Put the steps of the process-death test in the order it runs them.
hint: The four execute calls sit in the middle.
items: Send the app to the background with no return
Kill its process with am kill through the shell
Bring the app back with activateApp
Wait for the show's screen and check its title

prompt: Why does one rotation test per screen also cover the dark theme, the font size and the language?
hint: What does each of them do to the activity?

choices.text: Each one destroys the activity and creates it again
choices.why: Right. They reach the same code, so they share the same defects.

choices.text: Android applies them without touching the app
choices.why: Each is a configuration change, and the activity is rebuilt for it.

choices.text: Tickets has no dark theme or translations
choices.why: The activity is recreated whether or not the app draws anything different.

choices.text: They change the system's screens and not the app's
choices.why: They change the configuration every app's activity is drawn for.

prompt: Which of these interruptions can adb emu cause only on an emulator?
hint: adb emu talks to the emulator's console.

choices.text: The notification shade pulled down
choices.why: That is cmd statusbar, a shell command that works on any device.

choices.text: The back button
choices.why: input keyevent KEYCODE_BACK works on a phone too.

choices.text: An incoming call from a phone number
choices.why: Right. gsm call is a console command; a phone needs a real call.

choices.text: The dark theme
choices.why: cmd uimode night yes is a shell command, on any device.

prompt: Before reminder.test.mjs, somebody runs adb shell pm grant for POST_NOTIFICATIONS and removes the beforeEach. The Don't allow test now fails at waitUntilShown. Why?
hint: Read lines 32 to 34 of ShowActivity.kt again.

choices.text: pm grant takes effect after a reboot
choices.why: It takes effect at once; that is why the app no longer asks.

choices.text: Appium does not see the dialog without the beforeEach
choices.why: Seeing the dialog does not depend on a reinstall; there is no dialog to see.

choices.text: Already granted: nothing is asked
choices.why: Right. No request, no dialog: the test's starting state decides the path.

choices.text: The dialog's ids change after a grant
choices.why: The ids belong to Android's controller and do not depend on the answer.

prompt: states.test.mjs is run against a server started with npx appium --address 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. Where does the process-death test stop?
hint: Which of its calls needs a feature the server was not started with?

choices.text: At the session, which refuses UiAutomator2
choices.why: The session starts; only one command is refused later.

choices.text: At queryAppState, which answers 3
choices.why: It never gets there: the call before it fails first.

choices.text: At backgroundApp, which needs a shell
choices.why: backgroundApp is the driver's own command and needs no insecure feature.

choices.text: At mobile shell, which the server refuses
choices.why: Right. The shell runs any command on the device, so the server must allow it by name.

prompt: A person refused notifications on the show's screen. After which of these does the line remind_denied disappear, by the code's reading?
hint: The line is lost when the activity is recreated, and only then.

choices.text: Turning the phone to landscape
choices.why: Right. A rotation recreates the activity, and the visibility was not saved.

choices.text: Switching the phone to the dark theme
choices.why: Right. Another configuration change, the same recreation.

choices.text: Home, a process death, then back from Recents
choices.why: Right. The screen is rebuilt from the saved state, which has no visibility in it.

choices.text: Home and back, with the process still alive
choices.why: The activity was only stopped, so its views, the line included, are the same objects.

choices.text: Pulling the notification shade down and up
choices.why: The app stays underneath, unchanged.
